claims.text: Existing HEA intermediate layers are optimized for mechanical strength and single-phase stability.
Existing HEA intermediate layers have modest thermal conductivity under reactor conditions.
Adding approximately 5 wt% copper to the HEA will improve its heat-transfer capability.
Adding approximately 5 wt% copper will preserve the single-phase structural integrity required for the intermediate layer.
ML-assisted analysis of binary phase diagrams can predict whether HEAs form single solid solutions or phases containing intermetallics.
Phase-diagram analysis can identify composition bounds within which the copper-modified intermediate-layer HEA remains single phase.
Retention of a single solid-solution phase mediates the balance between enhanced thermal transport and structural integrity.
Copper addition increases the HEA's free-electron density.
The increased free-electron density produces more efficient heat transfer and higher thermal conductivity.
Keeping copper content low and within predicted phase-stable limits avoids precipitation of deleterious secondary phases.
Secondary phases would compromise the structural strength of the intermediate-layer HEA.
The copper-alloyed HEA will have significantly higher thermal conductivity than the unmodified HEA under the same operating conditions.
The copper-alloyed HEA will retain mechanical strength similar to that of the unmodified HEA.
The copper-alloyed HEA will retain phase stability under reactor operating conditions.
Copper remains in solid solution at concentrations up to approximately 5 wt% in the proposed HEA.
Exceeding approximately 5 wt% copper may induce secondary-phase formation and degrade structural performance.
The hypothesis is expected to hold at approximately 600–800°C under mechanical loadings typical of plasma-facing components.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and boundary require retention of a single phase, but the falsification rule treats secondary-phase formation as falsifying only when it also causes mechanical degradation. Secondary phases without detected degradation would violate the stated single-phase requirement but would not necessarily trigger the stated rule.
